name: secretsdump.py - DCSync (Linux)
description: Performs a DCSync attack using Impacket — impersonates a Domain Controller's replication partner to pull all NT hashes, Kerberos keys, and cleartext passwords (if reversible encryption used) from the domain. Requires the account to have DCSync rights: Replication-Get-Changes + Replication-Get-Changes-All on the domain object.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== HOW DCSYNC WORKS ===
DCSync abuses the MS-DRSR (Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol) that
Domain Controllers use to sync with each other. The attack:
  1. Connect to DC using credentials of any account with replication rights
  2. Issue GetNCChanges (DRSGetNCChanges) request — 'please replicate this object'
  3. DC responds with the object's attributes INCLUDING password hashes + Kerberos keys
  4. No code execution on the DC required — pure network protocol

This is why DCSync is so powerful: you never touch LSASS on the DC.

=== REQUIRED RIGHTS ===
The account you authenticate with needs BOTH:
  - DS-Replication-Get-Changes (Replication-Get-Changes)
  - DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (Replication-Get-Changes-All)
These are held by Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and the KRBTGT account itself.
Can be granted via ACL abuse (WriteDACL on domain object).

=== OUTPUT FILES ===
  outfile.ntds          → all NT hashes in user:rid:lmhash:nthash format
  outfile.ntds.kerberos → Kerberos keys (AES128, AES256, DES)
  outfile.ntds.cleartext→ cleartext passwords (only if reversible encryption enabled)

=== KEY FLAGS ===
  -just-dc              → DCSync only (skip registry dump, LSASS dump)
  -just-dc-user <user>  → pull only one specific account (quieter)
  -outputfile <prefix>  → saves to prefixed files above
  -hashes <lm:nt>       → pass the hash instead of password

=== WHAT TO DO WITH OUTPUT ===
1. Extract krbtgt hash → forge golden tickets (persistence)
2. Extract DA/EA hashes → pass-the-hash for DA access
3. Extract all hashes → spray + crack offline with hashcat -m 1000
4. Check for cleartext passwords (accounts using reversible encryption)

=== DETECTION ===
DCSync from a non-DC IP is anomalous — Microsoft Defender for Identity,
Splunk, and many SIEMs specifically alert on DRSGetNCChanges from non-DCs.
Event 4662 on the domain object with specific access GUIDs is the key log event.
High dwell = high detection risk. Move fast after gaining DCSync rights. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 22 (Attacking Active Directory Authentication).

defense.why_it_works: Identical protocol to Mimikatz DCSync but executed from Linux via Impacket's DRSUAPI implementation. secretsdump.py issues DRSGetNCChanges RPC calls to the DC using the provided account credentials; the DC validates the account has replication rights and returns password material including NT hashes, Kerberos keys (AES128/256/DES), and cleartext where reversible encryption is configured. No code runs on the DC — it is a legitimate replication response to a protocol-compliant request.
defense.prerequisites: Account with both DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All rights on the domain naming context. Network access to DC on TCP 135 and high RPC ports (49152+). Impacket installed. Credentials can be supplied as password, NT hash (-hashes), or Kerberos ticket (-k) — all three auth methods work.
defense.impact: Full domain credential extraction: all NT hashes (ready for pass-the-hash or offline cracking), all Kerberos keys for golden ticket creation, and cleartext passwords for accounts with reversible encryption. Output files (.ntds, .ntds.kerberos, .ntds.cleartext) are immediately actionable for further attacks. Compromise of KRBTGT enables persistent golden ticket access.
defense.detection: Windows Security Event 4662 on the domain object with replication GUIDs {1131f6aa, 1131f6ad, 89e95b76} from a non-DC source IP — the key indicator. A Linux IP connecting to DC on MSRPC/DRSUAPI is highly anomalous (DCs normally replicate with other DCs only). Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) generates a dedicated DCSync detection. Splunk/QRadar/Sentinel all have built-in rules for this event pattern. Event 4768/4769 from the Impacket client's Kerberos authentication preceding the replication call is also visible.
defense.artifacts: Event 4662 on target DC(s) with replication property GUIDs; MSRPC DRSUAPI network traffic from the attacking Linux host; output files on the attacker's disk (.ntds, .ntds.kerberos, .ntds.cleartext); Kerberos authentication events (4768/4769) if using -k mode.
defense.prevention: Audit and remove unnecessary Replicating Directory Changes All grants (should be DC machine accounts, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins only). Deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity for real-time DCSync alerting. Tiered administration to limit DA account proliferation. Network-level controls to restrict which hosts can reach DC RPC ports (allowlist DC-to-DC only where possible). Credential Guard on DCs.
defense.evasion: Use -just-dc-user to pull a single targeted account (much less network traffic than a full dump). Operate during business hours to blend with legitimate DC replication traffic. Pass-the-hash (-hashes) avoids sending the plaintext password over the wire. Event 4662 fires regardless of these measures — speed and immediate post-exploitation are the primary evasion.
defense.misconfiguration: User or computer accounts have been granted AD replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) that should belong exclusively to Domain Controllers. This right allows calling the MS-DRSR (Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol) to retrieve NTLM password hashes for any account — including krbtgt. Typically granted accidentally via WriteDACL on the domain object or through inherited ACEs.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Who has DCSync rights:
Get-ObjectAcl -DistinguishedName 'DC=corp,DC=local' -ResolveGUIDs |
    Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes'} |
    Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights

# Dangerous: any non-DC account appearing here
# CORP\svc_monitoring  DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All  <- not a DC
defense.secure_config:
# Remove non-DC replication rights:
# Using PowerView:
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=corp,DC=local' \
    -PrincipalIdentity 'svc_monitoring' -Rights DCSync

# Monitor with Event 4662 (Object access with properties):
# Filter for: ObjectType = DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All GUID
# {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}
# Any 4662 from non-DC account with this GUID = DCSync in progress

# Microsoft Defender for Identity: built-in 'DCSync attack' alert
# Anomalous AD replication from non-DC IPs also caught by MDI
